issues.body: bench_s3_trust_allows_ec2 returns success when it finds any matching Allow statement, without evaluating an overriding Deny or a Condition that excludes the launched instances. Its no-python fallback is weaker still: any occurrence of ec2.amazonaws.com passes, even in a Deny statement or alongside the wrong Action. cmd_check then prints that the policy “lets” EC2 assume the role and reports READY. This contradicts the README's claim that READY is based on a trust policy that actually lets EC2 call sts:AssumeRole, and permits manually drifted policy state to recreate the silent no-credentials/no-upload failure. Provision now writes a safe exact policy, but check is explicitly used as the readiness/drift check and must not overstate arbitrary effective policy documents.
issues.fix_hint: Either make check fail closed unless the trust document is exactly equivalent to the canonical bench_s3_trust_policy (the simplest fit because provision owns and overwrites this role), or implement the relevant IAM Deny/Condition semantics. Remove the substring fallback or fail closed when Python/another real JSON parser is unavailable. Add hermetic cases for an Allow plus overriding Deny, an Allow constrained by an incompatible Condition, and the no-python path; each must withhold READY.
issues.title: Trust check can still report READY for a role EC2 cannot assume

verdict.summary: Round 3 repairs the prior provisioning defect: an existing role is now converged with update-assume-role-policy, and the hermetic test proves the wrong-principal case is repaired before check becomes READY. However, the check-side trust predicate still knowingly accepts policies that do not actually permit EC2 assumption, despite the README and READY message claiming that stronger guarantee. This is materially the same load-bearing trust-validation finding at the same severity, so progress is stagnant.
